1.0.0.en: The rule of the judges: this is a period of 450 years after the death of Joshua the son of Nun, during which the Jews mixed with the surrounding pagans. God was angry with them, and the pagans occupied them and humiliated them. Then they repented, and God sent them a judge who ruled by His Law and delivered them from their enemies. Then they returned to mixing with the wicked, and God was angry with them a second time, and this story was repeated many times.

1.0.1.en: A famine: this is the famine that occurred in the days of Gideon (Judg 6:1-6, 11), because the Midianites and the Amalekites plundered the food of the Jews. This was a chastening from God because of their neglect of His Law and their mixing and intermarrying with the pagans.

1.0.2.en: Bethlehem-Judah: a village located south of Jerusalem at a distance of five miles. It is where Rachel died.. and in it Christ was born later. It was called Bethlehem-Judah because it lies in the portion of the tribe of Judah, to distinguish it from another village called Bethlehem, which lies in the portion of the tribe of Zebulun.

1.0.3.en: Moab: he was the son of Lot, and the Moabites were a people who troubled the children of Israel, and God commanded them not to mix with them. They lived east of the Jordan River.

1.0.4.en: In the days of the era of the judges, and specifically in the days of Gideon, a famine occurred in the land of Judah. One of the Jews could not bear it, so he emigrated to the pagan land of Moab, he and his wife and his two sons. This was a wrong act and contrary to the Law of God, for he did not seek God's guidance and went to a pagan people with whom God had commanded them not to mix (Deut 23:3). It was weakness of faith in the power of God, who is able to provide for him in the midst of the famine, especially since this famine was a chastening from God because of their neglect of His Law; it would have been better for him to repent and hold fast to the commandments of God.

1.0.5.en: If distress comes upon you, return to God with repentance and ask for His help, and do not rely on solving the problem with your material thoughts, lest you move further away from God. And trust that your God loves you and will not leave you in the midst of distress.

1.1.0.en: Elimelech: a name meaning "my God is king."

1.1.1.en: Naomi: a name meaning "pleasant of heart."

1.1.2.en: Mahlon: a name meaning "poverty and sickness."

1.1.4.en: Elimelech did not live according to his name, settling in his land and relying on God, but emigrated to the land of the pagans and took with him his wife Naomi, who lived according to her name, that is, she remained holding fast to her fellowship with God even in a foreign land, and all her longings were attached to returning to her country, where God is worshiped in the Tabernacle of Meeting. As for the names of his two sons, they express the bad condition, not only that which faced him in his own country, where there was famine, but even more the hunger and spiritual ruin that faced him in the land of Moab. It would have been better for him to remain in Bethlehem, which means the house of bread, and which signifies the spiritual bread that the children of God receive in their fellowship with Him.

1.2.0.en: God wanted to show His anger at this spiritually unsound act of emigrating to a land far from Him, whereby life with God becomes difficult. So the head of the family, Elimelech, died at a young age; he did not reach old age and did not enjoy the material goods that he wished to find in Moab, but his life was defiled by the evil surrounding him, and he died quickly.

1.3.0.en: Orpah: a Moabite name meaning "neck" or "back of the neck."

1.3.2.en: The two sons of Naomi married two Moabite women, contrary to the Law of God, which commanded keeping away from them (Deut 23:3), and they lived in married life for ten years and had no children by them. Here too God shows His anger at them, and does not give them fruit in a land foreign to the faith, because they left "Ephratah" (which is the old name of Bethlehem), whose meaning is fruit, a symbol of God's blessings to His children who hold fast to the spiritual life with Him. And the number ten signifies a complete period, that is, they did not obtain fruit however many long years they lived far from God.

1.4.0.en: God's anger reaches its fullness, and the two sons, Mahlon and Chilion, die, and so Naomi was left alone. Perhaps when a person feels loneliness he returns to God and finds his salvation, and this is what actually happened, as we shall see in the following verses, for Naomi thought of returning to her country.

1.4.1.en: And we notice here that Ruth did not bear children to her first husband, Mahlon, and this signifies the inability of the Law to offer salvation and blessing; but she bore later to Boaz, and from her offspring came Christ, and this signifies the ability of the Church in the New Testament to offer salvation and spiritual children. So Ruth in her former life is a type of the Church of the Old Testament, and then by her marriage to Boaz, of the Church of the New Testament.

1.5.0.en: Daughters-in-law: the daughter-in-law is the wife of the son.

1.5.1.en: News reached Naomi that the famine had ended in her country, so she thought of returning to Bethlehem, especially since she had become alone after losing her husband and her two sons. So she arose from her house to travel, and her two daughters-in-law went out with her to bid her farewell and to accompany her on the road of the journey.

1.6.0.en: Naomi thanked her two daughters-in-law for bidding her farewell and accompanying her some distance on the road of the journey, and with kindness and motherliness she asked them to be content with this distance and to return to the city.

1.6.1.en: And this shows, as will come in the following verses, that Naomi was distinguished by an overflowing love and motherliness that made her two daughters-in-law love her and cling to her. There was no human jealousy or attempt at domination in her fellowship with her daughters-in-law, so she was an example of a spiritual mother-in-law, that is, like a second mother. And Naomi asked God for blessings for them in appreciation of their love for her and for their husbands who had died. For Naomi appreciates feelings of love and gives thanks for them, and even asks God for blessings for those who love.

1.7.0.en: Naomi wished a happy marriage for her daughters-in-law, and this also shows her unselfishness in not refusing the marriage of her daughters-in-law to other husbands after her sons, for her motherliness seeks first the comfort of her daughters-in-law. And before this love between Naomi and her daughters-in-law, the feelings of all were moved and tears overflowed, and the sound of their weeping even rose.

1.7.1.en: The more love you offer to others, the more you win their souls, so that they want to cling to you, and consequently they learn from you the love of God and you guide them easily to the way of truth, even without words.

1.8.0.en: Her two daughters-in-law showed their attachment to her and declared that they would not leave her but would accompany her to live with her in her country. And this shows how great their love for her was, because she had first offered a great love that they had not heard of nor found among their own people. Thus the children of God appear different from the people of the world.

1.9.0.en: With love Naomi refused that they should accompany her, because she would not be able to provide husbands for them, for she was not pregnant, nor was it expected that she would bear sons who would grow up and marry them.

1.9.1.en: And Naomi here also, like Ruth in her first life, signifies the inability of the Law to offer salvation and sons and fruits. And she refers here to a practice of the Jews, that if someone died and had no children, his brother would marry his wife, and the firstborn son who was born would be reckoned to the deceased husband (Deut 25:5, 6).

1.10.0.en: The hand of the Lord is gone out against me: that is, He permitted my afflictions, which are the death of my husband and my two sons.

1.10.1.en: Naomi added that she had grown so old that it would not allow her a second marriage, and the hope that she would bear sons at this age was weak, and consequently she would not be able to provide husbands for them one day. Then she said that if it were possible for her to conceive sons, which is an impossible supposition, a problem would still remain: would her daughters-in-law wait many long years until the sons grew up and there was an opportunity for Orpah and Ruth to marry them?...! This of course is a very slight possibility. For all this she forgot her own need for her daughters-in-law to accompany her and thought of their comfort before her own.

1.11.0.en: Orpah was persuaded by her mother-in-law's words, so she kissed her and wept much and bade her farewell and returned to her city; but Ruth refused to bid her farewell and clung to her.

1.11.1.en: And here we find Orpah an example of human love, which appreciates the love of others but has limits, namely human reasoning, so she was persuaded and returned to her house. And so her name indicates this, for the name Orpah means the neck or the back of the neck, that is, she turned her back to her mother-in-law and went back to her place. But Ruth represents the divine love that God gives to His children, which surpasses human love and all reasoning, so she remained clinging to her mother-in-law.

1.12.0.en: Sister-in-law: the wife of the husband's brother.

1.12.1.en: In love and concern from Naomi for Ruth, she tried to prevent her from continuing the journey with her and asked her to return to her country and her gods like her sister-in-law Orpah. For although Naomi needed support because of her old age, she thought of Ruth's comfort before her own.

1.13.0.en: The LORD do so to me, and more also: a form of oath meaning that if I go back on my oath, I deserve a punishment greater than the ordinary.

1.13.1.en: The brilliance of Ruth's love for her mother-in-law appears, for she asked her not to repeat her pity for her and her invitation to return to her people, because Ruth's love surpassed all human love, and this appears in the following:

1.13.2.en: 1- Her clinging to her mother-in-law in her journey and in her dwelling in any place she chooses.

1.13.3.en: 2- Her acceptance to join the people of God and to leave the pagan people of Moab, that is, her desire to become a Jewess, having been influenced by the qualities of her mother-in-law and her faith.

1.13.4.en: 3- Her declaration of her faith in God and her leaving the pagan gods that the Moabites worship.

1.13.5.en: 4- Her insistence on being with her mother-in-law throughout her life, that is, until death, so that nothing can separate her from her mother-in-law except when God wills and one of them dies.

1.13.6.en: 5- Her hope in the eternal life that her mother-in-law hoped for, for even after death she wants to remain with her mother-in-law, so she asks to be buried in the place where her mother-in-law is buried.

1.14.0.en: Before the greatness of Ruth's love and her insistence on clinging to her mother-in-law, Naomi fell silent and no longer asked her to return to her country. And her heart was of course filled with joy, for she loved Ruth, so she rejoiced in her constant fellowship and in her acceptance to join the people of God and to believe in Him.

1.15.0.en: Naomi continued on the road, with Ruth accompanying her, until they reached Bethlehem, and when they entered the village after an absence of more than ten years, the whole village took an interest in welcoming Naomi, and this shows the following:

1.15.1.en: 1- The standing of Naomi as a devout person beloved by her relatives and neighbors.

1.15.2.en: 2- The change in Naomi's condition: she had gone out with three men, her husband and her two sons, and now she returns alone, accompanied by a young woman of a foreign race, and she has no possessions, whether cattle or anything else, that is, she gained nothing from her emigration but returned in a worse condition than she had been, so she deserved the pity and sorrow of the people of her village.

1.16.0.en: Naomi said to those of the village who met her, expressing her sorrow, that they should no longer call her Naomi but Mara, because God had permitted her to be chastened by her leaving her country, so many distresses came upon her, and this is their result, her return alone and poor... So she submits to God and to His chastenings, but she describes her state and her soul as bearing severe distresses.

1.17.0.en: Naomi continued her words and said that she went out from here to Moab and was full, for she had a husband and two sons, and now she returns empty after their death. And in faith she accepts the chastening of God, who humbled her and broke her, because she did not believe that she could live with Him and worship Him among her own people and sought material goods, and so she lost everything.

1.18.0.en: The Holy Bible specifies the time of the return of Naomi and Ruth to Bethlehem, which was the days of the barley harvest, which falls in the end of March and the beginning of April. And this was by the providence of God, who permitted a chastening for Naomi and Ruth but receives them with good among His people, because the days of harvest are wealth and good for the rich, and they also give to the poor who glean behind the reapers. And this was the beginning of the divine blessings for this sorrowful family, and other blessings followed after it until they were completed by the marriage of Ruth to Boaz, the great man, so that by her marriage she became the grandmother of Christ.

1.18.1.en: If God permits distresses for you, accept them with submission, and then, when God sees your obedience and your humility and your return to Him, He will pour out on you blessings you do not expect, and you will be compensated for all that you lost.

1.18.2.en: Ruth in the field of Boaz

2.0.0.en: This verse speaks about an important figure in this book, a man called Boaz, whose name means "mighty one." He is indeed a rich man of great standing in his town, strong in his position. And he was a relative of Elimelech, Naomi's husband. He is a type of Christ, who is able to do all things and supports His children however weak they are, and His heart is open with love to all, Jews and Gentiles, just as Boaz received in his field the poor of his own town and Ruth the Gentile.

2.1.0.en: Ruth heard from Naomi her mother-in-law about the Law of the Jews, which is that at their harvest, or the gathering of their produce, if some ears fell from the reapers during the harvest, they would leave them for the poor, who glean behind them to supply their needs (Deut 24:19-22; Lev 19:9, 10; 23:22). So she asked her mother-in-law to permit her to go and gather ears of barley behind the reapers, and she permitted her. And this shows two things:

2.1.1.en: 1- Ruth's diligence and her concern to work to find her sustenance and the sustenance of her mother-in-law.

2.1.2.en: 2- Her humility and good manners, for she asks permission of her mother-in-law in every work even though it is a good work and she takes responsibility from her to meet her needs and those of her mother-in-law.

2.2.0.en: Ruth went to search in the village for a barley field to glean behind the reapers, and God's providence led her to the field of Boaz, a relative of her husband.

2.2.1.en: God awaits your concern and diligence in order to help you with His grace and His providence until you find your salvation, for He rejoices in your striving and the intention of your heart and rewards you with many blessings.

2.3.0.en: Here the character of Boaz appears as a man who manages his properties with care and diligence, so he went out from his house to his fields to inspect the work of the harvest himself. And his kindness and love appear in his greeting to the reapers with a spiritual phrase, saying "The LORD be with you," that is, may God help you in your work and bless you. And the Church still uses this phrase in the Divine Liturgy, and the priest calls it out to the people, and they answer him just as the reapers answered Boaz, for they also said to him a beautiful spiritual phrase, "The LORD bless thee," that is, just as he wished for them the blessing of God, so they also return the greeting to him by wishing the blessing of God as well.

2.4.0.en: This verse shows Boaz's exactness in following up his work, for he had appointed a man in charge on his behalf to oversee the reapers in the field, and he followed with his eyes the reapers as they reaped and also the poor who glean behind them. And his attention was caught by a young woman who was a stranger to the town, for her clothes may have been different in addition to her appearance, so he asked his servant "Whose damsel is this?", that is, to which family does she belong; because a young woman is ascribed to her husband or her father or her master.

2.5.0.en: His servant told him that she was the Moabite damsel who had come back with Naomi, because the news had spread throughout all Bethlehem of Ruth's love and sincerity. And he called her a damsel because of her young age.

2.6.0.en: The house: a tent that they make in the field so that the workers may rest in it from the heat of the day. It may also be meant the house of Naomi.

2.6.1.en: The servant continued his words and said that Ruth came in the morning and asked permission to glean behind the reapers, and when they noticed her diligence and good manners, they also permitted her to glean among the sheaves that they were gathering to one side, from which some ears would fall, because the one who gleans must be trustworthy, or else she would take from the sheaves themselves. And this makes clear that Ruth had found grace in the eyes of the servant and the reapers, so they permitted her to do this. And her diligence also appears in that she was working all the time and rested only a little in the house, which was most likely a tent set up in the field.

2.6.2.en: And Ruth signifies the Church of the Gentiles, which sought Christ to find her salvation, and responded to His call and strove and so excelled over the Church of the Jews, which Naomi signifies, for she remained in the house because of her weakness. And the Church of the Gentiles found grace in the eyes of Christ and His servants.

2.7.s.en: (2) The dialogue of Boaz with Ruth

2.7.0.en: Hearest thou not, my daughter: a phrase meaning, listen attentively, my daughter.

2.7.1.en: The fatherhood of Boaz and his care appear in his concern for Ruth, for he called her and said to her, listen, my daughter, for she had changed from a stranger into a beloved daughter.. this is the grace of God given to His striving children. And he welcomed her to glean in his fields and even insisted that she not go to another field, lest anyone trouble her. And he charged his servants to take care of her and not to harm her, so he regarded her as one of the young women known to him and permitted to glean behind the reapers. And his tenderness also appears in that he permitted her to drink from the vessels of water from which the reapers drink if they thirst during the work in the heat of the day.

2.7.2.en: And the vessels of water signify the Church, from which the Holy Spirit overflows upon all who labor in the field of service and spiritual striving.

2.7.3.en: And Ruth's keeping close to the young women of Boaz signifies the spiritual person's sharing with his brethren in the Church in their spiritual striving, so that he is encouraged by them.

2.7.4.en: And the good treatment of Ruth by Boaz is due to:

2.7.5.en: 1- That he is a devout man who carries out the commandment of the Law concerning hospitality to strangers (Ex 23:9; Lev 19:33, 34).

2.7.6.en: 2- That he heard of her love and sincerity toward her mother-in-law and then her going out to work to meet her needs and those of her mother-in-law.

2.7.7.en: 3- That she is his relative through her husband.

2.8.0.en: Ruth marveled at this good treatment with which Boaz treated her, for she had not found the like of it in Moab in the way the people of the land treat strangers, so she bowed before him in appreciation of his love and said to him, what is this great grace that I have found in thine eyes.

2.9.0.en: When Boaz saw her humility and her appreciation of his love, he praised her for the following:

2.9.1.en: 1- Her sincerity and love in accompanying her mother-in-law and caring for her.

2.9.2.en: 2- Her leaving her father and mother and her people to live among a people foreign to her for the sake of caring for her mother-in-law and enjoying her fellowship.

2.10.0.en: Boaz continues his praise of Ruth for her leaving her pagan gods and her taking refuge in God, in whom she believed, to be sheltered under His care, so he asks God to give her the reward for this faith, which is the enjoyment of fellowship with God in addition to all the material blessings on earth.

2.11.0.en: Ruth thanked Boaz for his love and asked him to continue this grace for her, and declared that she had received great comfort through his love for her, which supported her in her trial, for she had lost her husband and lives in a foreign country and lives as a poor woman. And in humility she asked to be a handmaid to him, although she is a person of standing in her own country, but this is the humility that moves hearts with love toward the humble.

2.11.1.en: The more you humble yourself before people and thank them for their kindnesses and appreciate all their good works, the more you win their hearts and receive blessings from God and abundant love from people.

2.12.0.en: Vinegar: it is what is mixed with olive oil and resembles a salad.

2.12.1.en: Parched corn: tender grains of wheat that are roasted and then eaten either raw or cooked.

2.12.2.en: Boaz continued honoring Ruth, so he regarded her as one of the reapers working for him, and invited her at mealtime to eat bread with them and to dip it also in the vinegar, and he also gave her plenty of parched corn, and she ate and had some left.

2.13.1.en: Let fall: leave some ears to fall from the sheaves you have gathered as if they had fallen by accident on the ground, so that they would not embarrass Ruth.

2.13.2.en: After Ruth ate, she arose with diligence to continue her gleaning of the ears behind the reapers and also among the sheaves that they had gathered to one side, for Boaz and his reapers trusted in her faithfulness, and with love Boaz wanted to give her more ears, and so as not to embarrass her he told his reapers that when she walked behind them they should draw out some ears from the sheaves they were gathering and leave them to fall on the ground as if they had fallen by accident so that Ruth might gather more ears... It was a wonderful gentleness of feeling by which Boaz was distinguished.

2.14.s.en: (3) Ruth in the house of Naomi

2.14.0.en: Beat out: she struck the ears of wheat with a rod and separated the grain from the straw.

2.14.1.en: Ephah: a measure holding 22.9 liters, equal to about 17 kg of wheat.

2.14.2.en: Ruth continued gleaning the ears with diligence until evening, that is, the end of the day, and she gathered many ears, which she beat out and separated their grain alone, and the amount of grain was about an ephah of barley, which is a large amount that an ordinary young woman could not glean in a day, but it was the blessing of God and the generosity of Boaz. And this amount of barley is enough for the sustenance of Ruth and her mother-in-law for many days.

2.15.0.en: Ruth hurried to her mother-in-law's house to give her the barley she had gathered and also to give her some of what was left over after she had eaten of the parched corn and the bread. It is the feelings of love that do not want to eat alone but must share with her mother-in-law in what she eats.

2.15.1.en: May you feel for those around you, the members of your household and the poor, and let them enjoy what you enjoy, not only of material things, but also share with them what you enjoy of spiritual things, so that you tell them what you have heard about God and encourage them to be bound to the Church.

2.16.0.en: When Naomi saw the features of joy on Ruth's face and the good that she had brought from the field, she asked her about the field in which she had gleaned, and she blessed whoever met her while she was gleaning, because she rejoiced at the sight of her and at the good that was with her. So Ruth answered that she had gleaned in the field of a man called Boaz.

2.17.0.en: The kinsman: the nearest person to the deceased, who has the right to pay what is owed on the deceased's fields as a pledge, to restore his inheritance to him, and to marry his wife in order to raise up offspring in his name.

2.17.1.en: Naomi rejoiced that Ruth had gleaned in the field of Boaz and asked a blessing for him from God after she learned from Ruth all that he had honored her with, and she praised him because he had shown kindness to the living, namely Naomi and Ruth, and to the dead, namely Elimelech, Mahlon and Chilion, for his honoring Ruth is an honoring of Naomi and of her husband and her two sons who had died. And by this Naomi's appreciation of kindness and her thanks for it appear. Then she informed Ruth that Boaz is their second kinsman, that is, there is a kinsman nearer than he to Ruth, and then Boaz is the second kinsman.

2.17.2.en: And the first kinsman signifies the Law, which is unable to redeem us (as will become clear in ch. 4), while the second kinsman, that is, Boaz, signifies Christ, who redeemed us on the Cross.

2.18.0.en: Ruth also told Naomi about the good treatment of Boaz toward her, for he had invited her to continue gleaning grain in his fields until the end of the harvest, not only the barley harvest but also the wheat harvest that follows it.

2.19.0.en: Naomi rejoiced at this welcome from Boaz and urged Ruth to stay in his fields so as to find this good treatment and so that no one would harm her in strange fields.

2.20.0.en: Ruth obeyed with joy and continued gleaning the ears throughout the period of the barley and wheat harvest, and she would bring all that she gathered to her mother-in-law and take care of serving her.

2.20.1.en: Ruth is an example of perseverance, diligence, love and service to others. And she signifies those who strive spiritually throughout their lives until they attain the Kingdom.

2.20.2.en: Ruth at the threshing floor of Boaz
